newsitem.title: USA: USDA says new food safety measures kept E.coli in check.
newsitem.headline: USDA says new food safety measures kept E.coli in check.

text.p: New U.S. food safety measures including state-of-the-art computer surveillance for foodborne disease kept the recent E.coli outbreak from "exploding" throughout the nation, Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said on Tuesday.
Consumer groups acknowledge that the government has made strides in safeguarding the food supply but said the latest crisis highlighted loopholes that still exist in the system.

The USDA will hold a meeting on Wednesday with food service experts to discuss the safe cooking of hamburgers. Food safety experts say the dangerous bacteria is killed only by thoroughly cooking beef at 160 degrees Fahrenheit (71 C).

On Friday, the department said Arkansas meat processor Hudson Foods Inc would recall a record 1.2 million pounds of hamburger due to possible contamination with a deadly strain of the E.coli bacteria. Health officials blamed the bacteria for making 16 people sick in Colorado in July.

The last U.S. outbreak of the virulent E.coli O157:H7 linked to beef was in 1993, when 700 people got sick and four children died in the Pacific Northwest after eating undercooked contaminated hamburgers.

"Just look at the difference between this situation and what you had four years ago," Glickman told reporters after a speech. "We have to date kept the problem from exploding to a really serious problem that affected a lot of people."
"It is a test of the food safety monitoring and reporting system and it's working quite well," he said.

USDA is in the midst of implementing a revolutionary overhaul of federal meat inspection, replacing the "poke and sniff" method of certifying meat and poultry is safe to eat with scientific testing for sickness-causing bacteria, known as Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point systems (HACCP). Glickman also credited new safe-handling labels on meat and poultry and the cutting-edge computer system, Foodborne Disease Active Surveillance Network (FoodNet), which helps public health officials track foodborne disease.

"Absent the aggressiveness of the state of Colorado using part of FoodNet, we probably would have missed this and it could have been a much bigger problem," Thomas Billy, head of the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service, told Reuters.

"The new HACCP regulation definitely is an improvement on the system we had before but we are a long way from completely protecting consumers from contaminated food," said Heather Klinkhamer, spokeswoman for the group S.T.O.P., which stands for Safe Tables Our Priority.

Klinkhamer said one glaring flaw with last week's recall was that USDA does not have the authority to order mandatory recalls of defective products. She also said the Clinton administration needs to spend more to expand the FoodNet network from its current seven sites nationwide.

At sunrise on Monday, a team of inspectors from the Agriculture Department descended on the Hudson Foods meat-packing plant in Nebraska at the heart of the recall to try to determine the source of the E.coli contamination.

Investigators are also expected to visit the slaughter plants that supplied Hudson Foods with the beef. Animal feces that spills onto meat when the intestines are removed after slaughter is a major source of E.coli contamination.
"I think we should be able to say something here in two to three weeks' time," Billy said.
The strain of E.coli suspected of contaminating the beef patties can cause bloody diarrhea, dehydration, and in some, life-threatening kidney failure.
Since its discovery in 1982, E.coli O157:H7 has been blamed for thousands of illnesses and several deaths around the world in the past decade.

Last December, 15 people died and more than 200 others became ill in cases linked to contaminated meat served at a retiree luncheon in Scotland. And in Japan last year, 11 people died and nearly 9,000 others became sick from an outbreak of the E.coli strain.
